questions.q: Why does the same bug get explained two different ways to the two stakeholders?
options: There is no real reason; both versions should be word-for-word identical
The Operations Manager is not allowed to know the full details
Each audience has a different job to do with the information, even though the underlying facts are identical
The Sales Director's version should contain false information to simplify it
questions.explain: The framing and depth change by audience need, but both versions describe the same real incident.

questions.q: What does the Sales Director's version proactively answer, without her having to ask?
options: Which SQL Server instance hosts AdventureWorks2012
The internal display folder structure of the model
Whether anything she presented to leadership was wrong, and for how long
The exact DAX formula used in the fix
questions.explain: A business-impact framing anticipates the real question a time-constrained stakeholder will have and answers it directly.

questions.q: What does the Operations Manager's version include that the Sales Director's version doesn't need?
options: The actual mechanism — CALCULATE, ALL(TerritoryDim), and why the two measures coincidentally matched unfiltered
Instructions for installing SQL Server
A completely different, unrelated incident
A list of unrelated Power BI features
questions.explain: The Operations Manager reported the issue and will want the real technical explanation, since she may notice something similar again.

questions.q: What must stay identical between both versions of the explanation?
options: The exact sentence length
The number of DAX functions mentioned
Nothing needs to stay the same between the two versions
The facts: what was wrong, which numbers were affected, which weren't, and that it's fixed and validated
questions.explain: Framing and detail level can differ by audience, but the underlying facts must be consistent and accurate in both versions.

questions.q: Why is a simplified explanation that's also inaccurate a problem, not a solution?
options: Simplified explanations are always technically correct by definition
Simplifying for an audience should never mean changing the actual facts of what happened
Accuracy only matters for the Operations Manager, not the Sales Director
It isn't a problem as long as the Sales Director doesn't notice
questions.explain: The lesson draws a clear line: framing and depth can adapt to the audience, but the truth of what happened cannot change.
